title: batch-harmonizer-token-budget-adaptation-notes
content:
Purpose:
This note collects experiments and reasoning for a new lightweight controller we prototyped: the Batch Harmonizer (BH). BH adapts per-tenant effective batch size and timeout by reconciling two signals: a token-budget forecast and a deadline pressure multiplier. Goal: reduce p95/p99 tail for latency-sensitive tenants while holding overall token cost within 2% of baseline.

Background / motivation:
- Continuous batching is our dominant cost-saving mechanism, but it can create long tails for heterogeneous request lengths and tenant priorities.
- Existing heuristics (fixed max-batch + global timeout, urgency-weighted slots) reduce average latency but leave recurring tail spikes when a few long-token requests accumulate and cause head-of-line blocking.
- We want a quick adaptive layer that: (a) promotes small fast batches for tenants with high deadline pressure, (b) opportunistically aggregates when token forecasts suggest low contention, and (c) gracefully demotes runaway long-request tenants to avoid global tail amplification.

Key concept: Token Budget Adaptation (TBA) + Harmonization
- Token budget forecast: per-tenant short-horizon expected token demand (next 30s) estimated from moving-average token counts + peeked-inflight tokens. Implemented as EWMA on token_rate and token_variance.
- Deadline multiplier: per-tenant estimated deadline pressure computed from observed q90/ q99 latencies relative to SLA targets; multiplier >1 speeds flushes / lowers batch cap.
- Harmonizer policy: compute effective_batch_cap = clamp(base_cap * f(token_budget), 1, max_cap) then apply deadline_multiplier as a TTL-weighted override that lowers timeout and batch cap for the tenant. We also allow transient small-batch promotions for tenants whose recent requests are uniformly short.

Hypotheses:
1) BH reduces p99 by >20% for latency-sensitive tenants under mixed workloads without increasing total token throughput by >2%.
2) Token-budget forecasts will enable safe aggregation during idle tails and reduce small-batch penalties during low contention windows.
3) Deadline multipliers will prevent starvation of low-volume, time-critical tenants during bursts.

Experiment design:
- Workloads: three synthetic multi-tenant mixes run on dev-cluster-3 (8xA10G).
  - Mix A (read-heavy): 80% short (prompt tokens 20–60), 20% long (tokens 400–1200).
  - Mix B (even): 50/50 short/long.
  - Mix C (spiky): baseline short with periodic microbursts from 5 tenants sending 50 concurrent long requests.
- Tenants: 40 logical tenants, 6 marked latency-sensitive (SLA p95 < 120ms).
- Controllers compared: baseline (fixed cap=32, timeout=30ms), urgency-weighted (current prod), BH-v0 (token-only), BH-v1 (token + deadline harmonic), BH-v1-slowback (same but subtractive backoff for tenants exceeding token budget).
- Metrics collected: per-tenant p50/p95/p99 latency, batch size distribution, tokens served, GPU utilization, aborted/dropped requests, fairness index (Gini over latency), token-cost delta vs baseline.
- Instruments: microtrace annotations for batch formation, KV-cache warm hits, and scheduling decisions.

Setup and command snippets:
- Start harness: ./bench/run_multi_tenant --mix C --tenants 40 --sensitive 6 --duration 1800 --profile BH-v1
- Trace pull: ./bench/collect_traces --run BH-v1-2024-11-09 --out traces/BH-v1.tar
- Quick sample: tail -n 50 logs/scheduler.log | grep harmonizer | sed -n '1,200p'

Results (summary):
- Mix A: BH-v1 reduced p99 for sensitive tenants from 730ms -> 510ms (~30% improvement). Overall token cost +0.9%. p95 improved 18%.
- Mix B: modest gains, p99 down 17%, cost +1.4%. GPU utilization slightly higher during BH-v1 because of more aggressive small-batch promotion (fewer idle cycles wasted waiting).
- Mix C: biggest win for BH-v1-slowback: prevented two tenants from monopolizing batch window during microbursts. p99 for sensitive tenants dropped 42% (from 1.2s -> 700ms). Cost delta +1.7%.

Detailed observations and traces:
- Batch size distribution: BH-v1 shifted the median batch size for sensitive tenants from 18 -> 6, reducing head-of-line waiting but increasing kernel invocation frequency (~+9%).
- Timeout behavior: deadline multiplier effectively reduced per-tenant flush time from 30ms -> 8–12ms on high-pressure tenants. This cut queueing latency but raised small-batch overhead.
- Token-budget forecast accuracy: EWMA with alpha=0.2 predicted 1s ahead with mean absolute error ~12% for Mix A/B, but degraded to 25% error during spiky microbursts (Mix C). We mitigated by smoothing token_variance and imposing conservative caps.
- Fairness: BH-v1-slowback improved fairness index by 13% vs baseline in Mix C by imposing additive slowback when tenants exceeded 1.5x their forecast token_budget for 3 consecutive windows.
- Tail causality: microtrace revealed that many p99 events originated from cross-tenant interleaving where a long request entered an existing batch and lengthened execution; BH's demotion prevented these from forming large mixed batches.

Performance tradeoffs observed:
- CPU overhead: harmonizer controller added ~2–3% CPU on scheduler process and ~1% memory overhead for per-tenant counters. Acceptable for our infra.
- Kernel overhead: increased small-batch invocations led to ~6% increase in small-kernel calls which had negligible impact on GPU saturations for A10G cluster; for smaller GPUs this could matter.
- Cost vs latency: BH variants that were too aggressive on deadline multipliers reduced p99 further but increased overall token cost by up to 3.5%. We chose configs targeting <=2% cost delta.

Tunable knobs and recommended defaults (for prod trials):
- base_cap = 32 (unchanged), but effective_batch_cap clip range = [1, 24] for sensitive tenants.
- token_ewma_alpha = 0.2, lookahead = 1s window for forecasting.
- deadline_multiplier thresholds: 1.2 -> mild, 1.6 -> strong; TTL 2s.
- slowback trigger: exceed 1.5x forecast for 3 consecutive windows => additive backoff reduce effective_batch_cap by 30% for 5s.
- small-batch promotion threshold: last 3 requests length < 80 tokens -> preferential flush at 8–12ms.

Failure modes and risks:
- Forecast misestimation leading to oscillation: observed during Mix C when token variance spiked. Mitigation: increase smoothing and add hysteresis to slowback enable/disable transitions.
- Over-promotion: too many small-batch flushes increase kernel overhead and can degrade throughput for throughput-first tenants. Mitigation: tenant-level profiles (throughput_favor) to opt out.
- Edge GPUs: small kernels on low-memory GPUs had higher relative overhead. For Dedicated pools with smaller cards, tune promotion aggressiveness down.

Next actions / roadmap:
- Short (1–2 sprints): stabilize BH-v1 config, add dashboard panels (per-tenant effective_cap, token_budget forecasts, slowback events), run 48h soak on staging with simulated customer traffic.
- Medium (1 month): integrate BH into rollout pipeline as canary-only feature for a subset of customers; add automated regression tests that assert token-cost delta <2% for 95% of runs.
- Research: replace EWMA with light-weight probabilistic sketch (sampled token-length histograms) to improve burst forecasting accuracy without per-request overhead.
- Ops: add an operator override to pin effective_batch_cap per-tenant in console for enterprise debug flows.

Open questions:
- Optimal lookahead window: is 1s sufficient for real traffic patterns (we saw cases where 3–4s forecast would have helped)?
- Should we include model-context length heuristics (e.g., streaming generation vs finite response) into the harmonizer signal?
- Policy routing: can we combine harmonizer signals with smart routing (fallback to cheaper model variant) when forecast shows sustained high token demand?

Appendix: representative trace snippets and CSV excerpts (abridged)
- Batch formation timeline (tenant T-7): [t=0] request short(34) queued, [t=4ms] request short(28) queued, [t=10ms] flush (cap=8, timeout=12ms) -> dispatch (batch_size=2), backend_time=27ms, end-to-end = 42ms.
- Example slowback log: harmonizer:tenant=T-19 event=slowback trigger_ratio=1.78 window=3 decay_seconds=5 old_cap=16 new_cap=11
- CSV sample (sensitive tenant p99 by controller): baseline,730; urgency-weighted,620; BH-v1,510; BH-v1-slowback,480

Notes to reviewers:
- The BH prototype is intentionally lightweight and assumes per-tenant counters are kept off-heap in scheduler process; if we move to sharded schedulers we need to coordinate cross-shard slowback decisions.
- Please check the linked Confluence RFC for policy math and derivations.

If you want raw traces or the bench harness configs, say which run id and I will attach the tarball.

-- Lina
